extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and students of natural philosophy / mechanics (18th‑century popular science audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and experimental demonstration of foundational hydrostatical laws (pressure, buoyancy, communicating vessels) with optical and mechanical analogies; aimed to teach the principles by simple inexpensive experiments. Includes philosophical remarks about order in mechanics and the motions of light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particles of light obey precise optical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The innumerable particles (rays) issuing from each point of a flame, though mixed and crossing before reaching a glass, are afterwards collected after passing through the glass into distinct points that reproduce an inverted image of the flame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental demonstration: hold a spectacle‑glass between a candle and a paper; move the paper until a distinct inverted picture appears at ab. Observe cones of rays (A G L, B G L, etc.) and the confluent heap of particles at mn before the glass; note how after the glass the rays are collected again at a, b, c. Use this to argue that such precise ordered behavior of innumerable, very swift particles implies lawlike regulation (author uses this argument toward a teleological conclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics are consequences deducible from few natural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of motion consists of consequences deducible by argument from a few natural laws; bodies ignorant of why they move nevertheless observe the same laws with utmost exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance-style remark: Study classical mechanical treatises (Stevin, Wallis, la Hire) to see how many surprising effects follow from simple premises. The author uses this as a premise in philosophical arguments about design and authorship of laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology: 'liquids' and 'fluids' treated interchangeably here
rubrics_metrics.description: For brevity the author uses 'liquids' and 'fluids' to mean the same thing, though some reserve 'liquid' for water/oil and call air a fluid but not a liquid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: the text will not distinguish strictly between air and liquids in naming; readers may gloss 'fluid' as including both liquid and gaseous substances for the experimental discussions that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of a fluid yield to the smallest force and rejoin under gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: All the parts of a fluid, when at rest in a vessel, yield to the smallest force acting on them; separated parts immediately, by their gravity, come together again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical claim supported by everyday experience; used to justify manipulations in experiments and the assumptions of hydrostatics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free surface of a fluid becomes horizontal (level) under gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: The superficies of all fluids upon which there is immediately incumbent either another fluid or nothing heavy will, according to the action of gravity, become horizontal or level (parallel to the horizon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration: pour water and then oil of turpentine into a glass to see the horizontal plane between the two unmixable liquids; for small spatial extents the curved Earth surface may be approximated as a plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicating vessels / equal bore tubes reach same level
rubrics_metrics.description: In curve tubes of equal bore connected to the same body of fluid, the fluid will stand at the same height in each leg (e.g., to cause a fluid to stop at height AB in one side AI, you must fill the other side ID to the like height).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment: place a curved tube and straight tube into the same reservoir with equal lower orifices; when reservoir level is AB the fluid rises to same corresponding heights in both legs (used as introductory observation before formalizing pressure law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic pressure law (pressure on a horizontal area equals weight of the perpendicular column above it)
rubrics_metrics.description: If we suppose a horizontal plane through a quiescent fluid, the force whereby a part of it (e.g., PQ) is gravitated upon or press'd down is equal to the weight of the perpendicular column whose base is the area PQ and whose height is the vertical depth of fluid incumbent upon that plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental derivation: use curve tube YXQ and orifice PQ in a vessel; show that pressure on PQ is independent of vessel breadth and equals the weight of the column PQbg (the 'column of altitude'). Repeat by moving tube to different positions of the same horizontal plane; the stopping height inside the tube (de) demonstrates equality. This is the central proposition from sections XXIV–XXVI with stepwise experiments and thought experiments (inverted cup, varying vessel shapes) to illustrate independence from total mass or breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure at a depth depends on depth, not on breadth or total mass
rubrics_metrics.description: The pressure upon a part of a horizontal plane adapts most exactly to the depth (height) of the fluid above it and does not depend on the surface area or the total mass of fluid standing above that plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: place the same tube and orifice in a much larger vessel with the same depth; the pressure (as measured by stopping height in the tube) does not increase. The text emphasises that pressure is a function of vertical height (column) only, not of amount of fluid elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal pressure on equal areas at the same depth and transmission in all directions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every part equal to PQ of the horizontal plane is always press'd down with an equal force; likewise equal parts taken at pleasure are press'd upwards or downwards with the same force; a part pressed downwards experiences as much force as another equal part is pressed upwards (reciprocity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration: move the curve tube to various locations of the same horizontal plane and observe identical stopping heights; also thrust flat bottoms or objects under the surface and show that the local pressure equals the weight of the corresponding column, regardless of vessel shape. This is summarized in Sect. XXVII as a set of practical laws useful in hydrostatics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upward pressure (buoyant pressure) exists and equals weight of column of fluid beneath
rubrics_metrics.description: In stagnant fluids there is not only downward pressure but an actual upward pressure which adapts to depth (and is equal to the weight of the perpendicular column beneath); this upward pressure can suspend fluid in a tube and can raise lighter bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments: thrust an empty tube into water, stop its mouth, then lift out — the enclosed fluid remains suspended at a fixed internal level; remove the finger and the water may rise above external surface or oscillate until equilibrium. Use crooked tin tube and a light wooden lid to show water pushes upward and can hold the lid down until water insinuates between lid and tube and raises it. Quantitative inference: if the fluid inside neither rises nor falls, upward and downward forces equal, so the upward pressure equals the weight of the corresponding column (sections XXV–XXVI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium in stagnant fluid: upward and downward pressures equal
rubrics_metrics.description: If the fluid in a portion remains stationary, the upward and downward pressures acting there must be equal; if one prevailed the fluid would move according to that direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: enclose a column of fluid in a tube and compare its behavior when the external level is changed; the balance point where internal and external heights are equal demonstrates equality of upward and downward pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air behaves as a gravitating fluid and affects hydrostatical experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Air, being a fluid incumbent on water, exerts pressure that in some cases significantly alters outcomes (e.g., inverted glass holding water higher than external level). The effects attributed to vessel shape may often be due to air pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: inverted drinking-glass keeps internal water above external surface because of air pressing on external surface; use of air-pumps (vacuum) shows removal of air eliminates this support. In layered-fluid experiments include air as the uppermost fluid when determining columns of altitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different immiscible fluids lying on one another: pressures are determined by columns of all incumbent fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: When several unmixable fluids lie upon each other, the total perpendicular column of altitude consists of the vertical sum of the columns of each fluid incumbent upon a plane; pressure on a plane equals the weight of that entire column (the highest surface determines top of column).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment suggested: use two unmixable liquids (brine/pickle and oil of turpentine) and tubes to observe relative rise in legs; pour oil upon pickle and observe changes in tube levels. The author reports experiments with pickle and turpentine to demonstrate properties of different fluids acting upon one another and the role of air pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical recommendation: use simple, inexpensive experiments to demonstrate hydrostatic laws to beginners
rubrics_metrics.description: To give a true conception of hydrostatic meaning even to the most ignorant, the order of experiments should be simple, inexpensive, and presented in an order that builds from one liquid to several fluids acting together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's methodological guidance: begin with single-fluid experiments (water), then proceed to experiments with multiple fluids; present experiments in historical order as recorded in notes to make principles plain and intelligible to non-mathematicians (Sect. XXII).
